scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pachanga originated in Cuba in the late 1950s, specifically catalyzed by composer Eduardo Davidson's 1959 creation of the song 'La Pachanga' recorded with Orquesta Sublime.
It gained massive popularity across the Caribbean before being brought to the United States by Cuban immigrants during post-World War II economic and social upheavals.
Settling heavily in New York City's South Bronx, the music and dance exploded in venues like the Caravana Club and the Triton After-Hours Club.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social dance craze learned from friends and family in Cuban and New York Latin clubs, pachanga functioned as an expression of festive communal joy and cultural resilience among diaspora communities.
In the modern era, it serves as a performance showcase and technical training tool for advanced salsa and mambo dancers.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Pachanga is a grounded, happy-go-lucky dance featuring a Charleston-like flavor driven by the double bending and straightening of the knees.
Danced on the downbeat of four-four time to charanga instrumentation, the basic footwork mirrors mambo placement and weight shifts but incorporates a smooth glide instead of a tap.
A bounce originates in the knees, keeping them from ever completely straightening, while the upper body rocks and maintains posture.
Watch for Bronx Hop.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Described as a mixture of son montuno and merengue (or conga), pachanga music is festive, lively, and marked by jocular, mischievous lyrics.
It is traditionally performed by charanga ensembles—orchestras utilizing violins, flutes, horns, piano, bass, and drums.
Listen for the violin, flute, horns, drums.
The pulse is four-four time.

A festive, lively blend of son montuno and merengue featuring charanga instrumentation of violins, flutes, piano, bass, and drums, sounding very similar to cha-cha-chá but marked by a notably stronger downbeat and playful accompaniment riffs.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include Eduardo Davidson (composer), José Fajardo, Johnny Pacheco (creator of the Bronx Hop), Charlie Palmieri, and Orlando 'Landy' Perez.
Modern torchbearers and instructors include Eddie Torres, Eddie Torres Jr., Shani Talmor, and Melissa Rosado.
While born in Cuba and heavily developed in New York City's Latin scene, the style migrated and adapted globally.
Pachanga developed as an offshoot of charanga music, fusing son montuno and merengue (or conga).

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: pachanga is sibling of cha-cha-chá: Very similar in sound and era, though pachanga features a notably stronger downbeat and gliding footwork.
pachanga is influence of mambo: Pachanga mimics basic mambo step foot placement and weight shifts while dancing to mambo offbeat music.
pachanga is parent of son montuno: Pachanga music is described as a mixture of son montuno and merengue.
pachanga is parent of merengue: Combined with son montuno to form the core musical identity of pachanga (also called merenconga).
